content:
Mr Chan and Mrs Chan's unit in Wang Shing House was undamaged. The day before they sold their title, a narrator even phoned Mrs Chan, promising she could soon return to the flat to pack up, and told her to sign the agreement with peace of mind.

Witnessing Wang Fuk Estate rise from the ground—courting here, raising grandchildren here

At the end of 1982, Mr Chan and his girlfriend, with whom he planned to marry, took a diesel train to Tai Po to inspect the yet-to-be-completed Wang Fuk Court. Being the pioneer estate in Tai Po's newly reclaimed area, its per-foot price was cheaper than the Home Ownership Scheme estates King San Court and Yan Tsui Court of the same period. "I myself have an attachment to it—Tai Po was the place I often cycled to when I was a boy." Mrs Chan suggested choosing the sea-facing blocks: "Block G (Wang Shing House) is sandwiched between two towers, it feels safer."

The following year, the Kowloon-Canton Railway was fully upgraded to electric trains, and Wang Fuk Court was officially occupied. When Mr Chan and Mrs Chan married in 1985, the Tolo Highway was also opened to traffic. Mrs Chan recalled that her husband, fearing the wind on Tolo Highway would be too strong for the bridal car, had stayed up all night sewing the bridal gown of the car-head doll tightly with needle and thread. The memories are sweet. Soon their son and daughter were born in succession, and the once-unfamiliar and desolate Tai Po became the roots of the Chan family. Up until the couple's semi-retirement to care for grandchildren in recent years, the home in Wang Shing House has borne the footprints of four generations.

Unaware of the fire at Wang Shing — only fled 55 minutes later

Having lived there all along, until the afternoon of 26 November last year, Mrs Chan heard an explosion in the kitchen. She looked out the window and saw nothing unusual. At 3 p.m., Mr Chan found the wireless network could not connect, turned off the television and took a nap, only to hear a commotion half an hour later. He went downstairs to take a look and saw firefighters hurrying past, but from his angle he could only see smoke at Wang Cheong House, and heard no alarm bells. He went home and leaned casually against the sofa, saying: "The next building is on fire." Just then Mrs Chan received a call; their anxious son said Wang Fuk Court was on fire, and she still soothed him by saying the fire was not on their side. They did not know that by then, the scaffolding netting on Wang Shing House had already caught fire.

Mrs Chan looked at her husband's calm expression, recalled the panic in her son's voice, and felt something was wrong. She called the management office to confirm; the staff also said the neighbouring block was on fire, but because of strong winds on site, they advised them to close the windows and leave home for safety. Mrs Chan recalled that smoke began appearing in the corridor, and the couple discovered the fire hydrant was dry. Just as they were hesitating whether to take the stairs, the lift doors happened to open, and they decisively stepped in.

According to records, Wang Shing House's earliest time of fire was exactly three o'clock. Mr and Mrs Chan escaped the building at 3:55 p.m., and looked back in shock to see fireballs bursting out of Wang Sun House, with multiple fire fronts blazing across the estate.

Soul lost after the disaster — "Why am I here?"

The fire took the lives of 168 people. Mr and Mrs Chan narrowly escaped and are temporarily staying at the Hong Kong Housing Society building in Hung Shui Kiu. They have tidied their temporary home neatly, maintaining the habits they had at Wang Fuk Court—cycling in and out, using air-conditioning sparingly, getting through the sweltering summer with mosquito nets and fans. "Wang Fuk Court had lovely breeze."

Mrs Chan relies on her faith to face the great change with strength, but occasionally drifts off: "Suddenly I think, why am I here?" When Mr Chan returns to Tai Po for work, he also looks at the crowds blankly: "Watching people go home, where is my home?" Some neighbours had mental breakdowns after going upstairs; others poured out their woes to them, saying they wanted to cry every time they woke up.

Self-made "Waiting for Justice, Wang Fuk kids meet again" T-shirts to speak out

For a period of time, Mr Chan held onto hope of rebuilding Wang Fuk Court: "At first I thought he was just talking big, let's wait, wait for the report, see how bad the damage is. Since nothing came out one after another, that means there's no hope." He wrote his heart on white T-shirts: I ♡ Wang Fuk, Forever a Wang Fuk person, Waiting for Justice, We wanna go Wang Fuk, Not Ideal? But >168 were killed! One of them reads "苑子蟲見" (Wang Fuk kids meet again), with the character 蟲 (caterpillar) replaced by a drawing of the estate's landmark caterpillar climbing frame.

They wore the T-shirts to express their stance when going upstairs, but as time went on, the government's message became clearer and clearer—residents would not be rehoused on the original site. Mr Chan refuses to accept it: "Block G died with unclosed eyes. You can say it was burned to the ground, then forget it, but that's not the case. It's still here, still usable, yet it's gone. That feeling is... you can't grasp reality, unhappy, so unhappy."

Selling the title still cannot arrange future life

He criticised that the post-disaster arrangements lacked a human touch and fell below expectations. For example, when they went upstairs, the authorities had not prepared lighting, leaving residents to grope in the dark while packing; nor was there any option of using equipment to help elderly residents reach the upper floors. On the other hand, information after selling the title was unclear—residents were not guaranteed to be able to choose a flat smoothly. "There's no price, no orientation, no idea how the ballot works—how can I arrange my life?"

Mrs Chan has been haunted by nightmares, dreaming of someone forcibly snatching the object she clutches tightly in her hand, unable to sleep at night. "If we don't sign, what can we do? It's not that we wanted to compromise from the start, but if you don't compromise, they'll play you even more. After 8.31 [the 2019 Yuen Long attack], what do you fear they won't do? From the beginning they knew people needed to unite, they wouldn't let us unite—without unity there's really nothing." Reluctantly, they decided to sell their title, hoping to put down some of the pressure for now. "Hong Kong is no longer the Hong Kong we knew. What can we do?"

Narrator promised they could go upstairs again—only knew there was no arrangement after signing

Having only ever bought a property once in her life, Mrs Chan was especially frightened by the clauses of the government's sale and purchase agreement, worrying she would bear legal responsibility if the government failed to acquire all titles smoothly, and fearing that selling the property meant giving up all uncollected belongings at home. She repeatedly pressed the narrator on when she could return home to pack, saying she could not sign the agreement with peace of mind for this reason. The day before signing, the narrator returned her call, saying Financial Secretary Deputy Mr Wong Wai-keung had promised to arrange another visit upstairs soon, and told her to sell the property without worry. To their surprise, after signing, the social worker replied that there was no arrangement for going upstairs for the time being. Mrs Chan felt deceived, but had nothing more to say.

Although they have left, they are forever Wang Fuk people. They still often recall the scene of that day's fire, keep close tabs on Wang Fuk Court's investigation reports, and hope in the future to buy into Yan Yuet Court in the same district, staying on in Tai Po. "We can't let go, but we can't do anything about it. At least there are several thousand people keeping us company."
